patient.name: Kwame Mensah
patient.setting: GP surgery, then colorectal outpatient clinic
patient.complaint: Bright red blood on the toilet paper and a lump that comes down after he opens his bowels
background: Accountant in Croydon; sits all day
No weight loss; no family history of bowel cancer

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with painless bright red bleeding (internal) versus a painful purple lump (thrombosed external), with anal fissure and cancer as distractors; grading by prolapse is also asked.

points: Kwame, 46, has **bright red blood** on the paper and dripping into the pan.
Blood **coats** the stool; it is not mixed in.
A soft lump comes down after each motion; he **pushes it back** with a finger.
It is **painless**; some itching and mucus.

steps.lead: Kwame's bleeding comes from **dilated vascular cushions** in his anal canal: normal structures that have become symptomatic.
Kwame strains with **constipation**, is **obese** and eats little fibre: the classic set. He has **no systemic symptoms**.
Painless, bright red bleeding coating the stool, itch and prolapse on straining that needs **manual reduction**: **internal haemorrhoids, grade 3**.

visual.title: Haemorrhoid grade
visual.label: Kwame grade 3
visual.caption: Grade is set by what the haemorrhoid does when he strains.

steps.q: Kwame's lump prolapses on straining and he has to push it back. What grade?
steps.r: **Grade 3** needs manual reduction. Grade 2 goes back by itself; grade 4 cannot be reduced.

steps.title: Internal vs external vs fissure
head: Feature
Internal haemorrhoid
Thrombosed external
Anal fissure
rows: Bright red, coating stool or dripping

steps.lead: If Kwame ever gets **sudden severe pain** with a **purple, tender lump** at the anal margin, that is a **thrombosed** haemorrhoid.
Months of daily bleeding could make Kwame **anaemic**; thrombosis, ulceration and prolapse are the other complications.

steps.text: Painless bright red blood in someone **over 50**, or with weight loss or change in bowel habit, is not 'just piles' until the colon is checked.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is clinical examination with proctoscopy, or flexible sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy if there are red flags.

points: Inspection: no external lump at rest.
DRE: **no palpable abnormality**; no blood mass, no tenderness.
Proctoscopy: engorged cushions at **3, 7 and 11 o'clock**.

steps.lead: Kwame's **DRE is negative** because internal haemorrhoids are soft and sit high; **proctoscopy** shows them.

steps.q: Kwame's DRE is normal. Does that rule out haemorrhoids?
o: No: internal haemorrhoids are often impalpable
No: only CT can show them
steps.r: Soft internal cushions are often not felt. **Proctoscopy** is the way to see them.

steps.title: Kwame's bloods
steps.text: No anaemia, so no sign of significant chronic blood loss.

visual.title: Haemoglobin
visual.label: Kwame 139
visual.caption: Normal: his bleeding has not caused anaemia yet.

steps.lead: Kwame is 46 with typical features and **no red flags**, so no scope is needed. Weight loss, change in habit or doubt would mean **flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy**.

steps.text: Proctoscopy is the bedside test for haemorrhoids; scopes are for **red flags** or **diagnostic uncertainty**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' driven by grade: conservative and topical for grade 1, rubber band ligation for persistent grade 1 to 3, haemorrhoidectomy for grade 3 to 4, and conservative care for a thrombosed haemorrhoid.

steps.lead: Everyone starts with **fibre, fluids and no straining**; Kwame starts **ispaghula husk**. Topical **hydrocortisone** is for grade 1 (not in pregnancy, where **Anusol** is used).

steps.q: Kwame's grade 3 haemorrhoids still bleed after 6 weeks of fibre and fluids. Next step?
steps.r: **Rubber band ligation** via a proctoscope is the procedure for persistent grade 1 to 3, mainly grade 3.

steps.lead: Kwame has **rubber band ligation** in clinic; sclerotherapy (grade 2), infrared photocoagulation or a stapled haemorrhoidopexy are alternatives.

visual.title: Kwame's bleeding episodes per week
visual.caption: Fibre helps a little; banding stops the bleeding.

steps.lead: If Kwame's haemorrhoids return as **grade 3 to 4** despite banding, **haemorrhoidectomy** is definitive.

points: Six months later: **sudden severe anal pain** for 2 days.
Purple, tense, very tender lump at the anal margin.

steps.lead: Kwame's thrombosed haemorrhoid is managed with **analgesia, stool softeners and ice packs**; excision only if severe.

steps.text: Topical **hydrocortisone** is contraindicated in **pregnancy**: use an emollient such as Anusol, fibre and fluids.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why internal haemorrhoids are painless (above the dentate line, visceral innervation), why portal hypertension worsens them, or how banding works.

steps.lead: Years of **straining** raised Kwame's intra-anal pressure until his normal anal cushions engorged and slid down.
Kwame's banding did not hurt because it was **above the dentate line** (visceral nerves). His thrombosed lump hurt because it was **below** it (somatic nerves).

o: Somatic innervation above the dentate line
Visceral innervation above the dentate line
steps.r: Above the dentate line the mucosa has **visceral** innervation, which does not sense cutting or banding as sharp pain.

steps.lead: If Kwame had **cirrhosis**, **portal hypertension** would raise pressure in the haemorrhoidal plexus and worsen bleeding.
Kwame's band cut off blood supply: **ischaemic necrosis**, then the tissue **sloughs off** and fibrosis fixes the cushion.

prompts.q: What are haemorrhoids, where are they, and who gets them?

points.p: Dilated vascular cushions in the anal canal
At 3, 7 and 11 o'clock
Constipation, straining, pregnancy, obesity, low fibre
Bright red bleeding coating stool or dripping into the pan
Painless
Pruritus, mucus, incomplete emptying, prolapse after defecation

points.p: 1: no protrusion
2: protrudes on straining, reduces spontaneously
3: needs manual reduction
4: permanently prolapsed, irreducible

prompts.q: How does a thrombosed haemorrhoid present and what complications can haemorrhoids cause?

points.p: Sudden severe anal pain, purple, oedematous, tender lump
Complications: anaemia, thrombosis, ulceration, prolapse

prompts.q: How are haemorrhoids diagnosed, and when do you scope?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a normal DRE does not exclude them.

points.p: Clinical with proctoscopy
Internal: often negative DRE; external: tender lump on DRE
points.why: Internal sit high and are soft.

points.p: Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy for red flags or doubt
points.why: Weight loss, change in habit, older age.

prompts.q: What is the conservative and topical management?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: pregnancy changes the cream.

points.p: Fibre, fluids, avoid straining; ispaghula husk
Grade 1: topical hydrocortisone
Pregnancy: topical emollient (Anusol)

prompts.q: Which procedures are used for which grade?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: band 1 to 3, cut 3 to 4.

points.p: Rubber band ligation: persistent grade 1–3, mainly 3
Sclerotherapy (grade 2), infrared photocoagulation, stapled haemorrhoidopexy
Haemorrhoidectomy for severe grade 3–4

prompts.q: How do you manage a thrombosed haemorrhoid and when is it urgent?

points.p: Analgesia, stool softeners, ice packs
Excision if severe
Urgent review: severe bleeding, thrombosis or strangulation

prompts.q: Why are internal haemorrhoids painless and external ones painful?

points.p: Internal: above dentate line, columnar mucosa, visceral innervation
External: below dentate line, squamous, somatic innervation

prompts.q: What causes haemorrhoids, why does liver disease worsen them, and how does banding work?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: pressure and blood supply.

points.p: Raised intra-abdominal/intra-anal pressure engorges the cushions
Portal hypertension raises haemorrhoidal plexus pressure
Banding: ischaemic necrosis, fibrosis, sloughs off

glossary.haemorrhoids: Engorged, symptomatic vascular cushions in the anal canal.
glossary.vascular cushions: Normal pads of blood vessels and connective tissue that help seal the anus.
glossary.dentate line: The line in the anal canal dividing visceral (painless) above from somatic (painful) below.
glossary.internal haemorrhoids: Haemorrhoids above the dentate line; painless, bleed bright red.
glossary.external haemorrhoids: Haemorrhoids below the dentate line; painful, especially if thrombosed.
glossary.thrombosed haemorrhoid: A haemorrhoid with clotted blood inside; purple, tense and very painful.
glossary.prolapse: Slipping down and out of normal position, here through the anus.
glossary.manual reduction: Pushing a prolapsed haemorrhoid back in with a finger.
glossary.lithotomy position: Lying on the back with hips and knees flexed; used for clock-face positions.
glossary.proctoscopy: Viewing the anal canal and lower rectum through a short rigid tube.
glossary.proctoscope: A short rigid tube used to inspect the anal canal.
glossary.DRE: Digital rectal examination with a gloved finger.
glossary.flexible sigmoidoscopy: Camera examination of the rectum and sigmoid colon.
glossary.colonoscopy: Camera examination of the whole colon.
glossary.ispaghula husk: Bulk-forming laxative that softens stool and reduces straining.
glossary.Anusol: A soothing topical haemorrhoid preparation suitable in pregnancy.
glossary.hydrocortisone: Topical steroid used for grade 1 haemorrhoids; avoided in pregnancy per the notes.
glossary.rubber band ligation: A tight band placed at the base of an internal haemorrhoid so it dies and falls off.
glossary.sclerotherapy: Injection of a sclerosant to scar and shrink a haemorrhoid.
glossary.infrared photocoagulation: Heat applied to a haemorrhoid to scar its blood supply.
glossary.stapled haemorrhoidopexy: Stapling procedure that lifts prolapsed haemorrhoids back into place.
glossary.haemorrhoidectomy: Surgical excision of haemorrhoids; definitive for severe grade 3 or 4.
glossary.ischaemic necrosis: Tissue death from loss of blood supply.
glossary.strangulation: Cut-off blood supply to prolapsed tissue; an emergency.
glossary.portal hypertension: Raised pressure in the portal venous system, usually from cirrhosis.
glossary.visceral innervation: Autonomic nerve supply that senses stretch, not cutting or pinching.
glossary.somatic innervation: Nerve supply that senses sharp pain and touch precisely.
glossary.anal fissure: A painful tear in the anal lining, usually posterior midline.
glossary.perianal abscess: A collection of pus beside the anus; red, hot and fluctuant.
glossary.tenesmus: A feeling of incomplete emptying or needing to go when the rectum is empty.

technique.stem: A 38 year old woman has 2 months of bright red blood dripping into the toilet after opening her bowels. It is painless. She has been constipated since the birth of her second child. She has no weight loss. Abdominal and rectal examinations are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about rectal bleeding: decide pain or no pain, mixed or separate.
Painless, bright red, dripping, constipation, normal DRE: internal cushions.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Internal haemorrhoids.**

elim: Would be painful on defecation with a visible tear.
Young, no weight loss or change in habit; blood is on the outside.
Would be felt on DRE; painful if thrombosed.
Bloody diarrhoea with urgency, not dripping blood with constipation.

steps.x: **D. Internal haemorrhoids.** Painless bright red blood + normal DRE = internal haemorrhoids.

technique.stem: A 41 year old man has intermittent painless bright red rectal bleeding and itching. He has no weight loss or change in bowel habit. Rectal examination is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: Confirming the diagnosis when DRE is normal.

clues: painless bright red rectal bleeding and itching
no weight loss or change in bowel habit
steps.x: Classic internal haemorrhoids, no red flags; DRE misses them.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Proctoscopy.**

elim: For incomplete colonoscopy or frail patients with suspected cancer.
For red flags or diagnostic doubt.
For fistulae or rectal cancer staging.

steps.x: **E. Proctoscopy.** Internal haemorrhoids: DRE often normal, proctoscopy shows them.

technique.stem: A 33 year old man has 2 days of severe anal pain. There is a 1 cm purple, tense, very tender lump at the anal margin. He is otherwise well. His temperature is 36.8°C.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Analgesia, stool softeners and ice packs
Incision and drainage under general anaesthetic

steps.x: Initial management of an acutely painful anal lump.

clues: purple, tense, very tender lump at the anal margin
steps.x: Thrombosed external haemorrhoid: conservative measures; excision only if severe.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Analgesia, stool softeners and ice packs.**

elim: For a perianal abscess with a hot, fluctuant swelling.
For internal haemorrhoids above the dentate line; would be agony here.

steps.x: **A. Analgesia, stool softeners and ice packs.** Thrombosed = conservative first.

technique.stem: A 57 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has troublesome bleeding haemorrhoids. He has ascites and splenomegaly.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism worsening his haemorrhoids?

steps.x: Mechanism: link the liver to the anal cushions.
Portal hypertension raises pressure in the haemorrhoidal plexus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Raised portal venous pressure.**

elim: Worsens bleeding but does not engorge the cushions.

steps.x: **C. Raised portal venous pressure.** Portal hypertension engorges the haemorrhoidal plexus.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man has 3 weeks of bright red blood coating his stools and on the toilet paper. It is painless. He also has itching. He strains because of constipation. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Abdominal and rectal examinations are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Painless bright red blood coating the stool with pruritus and constipation is internal haemorrhoids; DRE is often normal.

steps.x: Diagnosis of rectal bleeding.

clues: bright red blood coating his stools
steps.x: Painless bright red coating blood, pruritus, straining.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Internal haemorrhoids.**

elim: Severe pain with a purple lump.

steps.x: **C. Internal haemorrhoids.** Painless = above the dentate line.

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman has 1 day of sudden, severe anal pain. She has a 1.5 cm purple, oedematous, very tender lump at the anal margin. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden severe pain with a purple, tender lump at the anal margin is a thrombosed external haemorrhoid; an abscess is red, hot and fluctuant.

steps.x: Diagnosis of an acutely painful anal lump.
Sudden pain, purple tender lump, afebrile.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thrombosed external haemorrhoid.**

elim: A tear, not a lump; pain with defecation.
In the natal cleft, not the anal margin.

steps.x: **E. Thrombosed external haemorrhoid.** Purple + tender + sudden = thrombosed.

practice.stem: A 51 year old man has haemorrhoids that come down when he opens his bowels. They stay down until he pushes them back with his finger. Colonoscopy last month was normal. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the grade of his haemorrhoids?
practice.e: Haemorrhoids that prolapse on straining and need manual reduction are grade 3.

steps.x: Grading: what happens on straining?

clues: come down when he opens his bowels
pushes them back with his finger
steps.x: Prolapse on straining needing manual reduction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Grade 3.**

elim: Full-thickness rings of rectum, usually elderly; colonoscopy-normal man with known haemorrhoids.

steps.x: **C. Grade 3.** Manual reduction = grade 3.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has painless bright red bleeding after defecation. Proctoscopy confirms internal haemorrhoids.
practice.q: Which is the most likely position of the haemorrhoids, with the patient in the lithotomy position?
practice.e: The three main anal cushions sit at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock in the lithotomy position.

steps.x: Anatomy of haemorrhoids.
Anal cushions sit at left lateral, right posterior and right anterior.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **3, 7 and 11 o'clock.**

elim: Common site for a fissure (anterior), not haemorrhoids.
Classic posterior site of anal fissure.

steps.x: **C. 3, 7 and 11 o'clock.** 3, 7, 11 = cushions; 6 = fissure.

practice.stem: A 36 year old man has 2 years of near-daily painless rectal bleeding from proctoscopy-proven grade 3 haemorrhoids. He feels tired. A recent colonoscopy was normal. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his tiredness?
practice.e: Months of haemorrhoidal bleeding with a normal colonoscopy and microcytic anaemia with low ferritin is iron deficiency from chronic blood loss.

steps.x: Cause of a complication.
Chronic bleeding with microcytic, low-ferritin anaemia and a clear colon.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Iron-deficiency anaemia from chronic bleeding.**

elim: Ferritin would be normal or high.

steps.x: **E. Iron-deficiency anaemia from chronic bleeding.** Anaemia is a complication of chronic haemorrhoidal bleeding.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant has painless bright red blood on the toilet paper and a soft lump that comes down when she strains and goes back by itself. She has been constipated during pregnancy.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pregnancy and constipation are classic causes; a painless lump that prolapses and reduces spontaneously is grade 2.

steps.x: Diagnosis and grade.
Pregnancy and constipation, painless bleeding, spontaneously reducing prolapse.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Grade 2 internal haemorrhoids.**
**C. Grade 2 internal haemorrhoids.** Reduces itself = grade 2.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man has 6 weeks of rectal bleeding which he puts down to his known haemorrhoids. His stools have become looser and he has lost 4 kg. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg. Proctoscopy shows grade 2 haemorrhoids.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: Haemorrhoids do not cause weight loss or change in bowel habit; with red flags the colon must be examined by colonoscopy.

steps.x: Next investigation: are there red flags?
Haemorrhoids do not explain weight loss and change in habit over 60.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Colonoscopy.**

elim: Does not look at the mucosa.
For IBD vs IBS in younger patients.

steps.x: **B. Colonoscopy.** Red flags mean scope the colon even if haemorrhoids are seen.

practice.stem: A 39 year old man has painless bright red bleeding on the paper and a sensation of incomplete emptying. Rectal examination is normal. He has no red flag features.
practice.q: Which finding on proctoscopy is most likely?
o: Engorged cushions above the dentate line
Purple tender lump below the dentate line
practice.e: Painless bleeding with a normal DRE points to internal haemorrhoids, seen on proctoscopy as engorged cushions above the dentate line.

steps.x: Expected proctoscopy finding.
Painless bleeding + normal DRE: internal haemorrhoids above the dentate line.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Engorged cushions above the dentate line.**
**A. Engorged cushions above the dentate line.** Internal = above the dentate line.

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman who is 26 weeks pregnant has itchy, bleeding grade 1 haemorrhoids. She is constipated. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 112/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Fibre, fluids and a topical emollient
practice.e: In pregnancy, grade 1 haemorrhoids are managed with fibre, fluids and a topical emollient such as Anusol; hydrocortisone is avoided.

steps.x: Initial management in pregnancy.
Conservative measures plus a soothing emollient (Anusol); avoid steroids.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Fibre, fluids and a topical emollient.**

elim: Grade 3–4 only, and avoided in pregnancy.
Contraindicated in pregnancy per the notes.

steps.x: **A. Fibre, fluids and a topical emollient.** Pregnant: Anusol, not hydrocortisone.

practice.stem: A 48 year old man has grade 3 haemorrhoids that still bleed and prolapse after 3 months of a high-fibre diet and ispaghula husk. He is otherwise fit. His temperature is 36.7°C and BP 130/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: Persistent grade 1 to 3 haemorrhoids after conservative treatment are treated with rubber band ligation; haemorrhoidectomy is for grade 4 or failure.

steps.x: Next step after conservative treatment fails.

clues: after 3 months of a high-fibre diet and ispaghula husk
steps.x: Persistent grade 1–3 (mainly 3): banding.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Rubber band ligation.**

elim: Reserved for grade 4 or failed banding.

steps.x: **C. Rubber band ligation.** Fail conservative → band → surgery.

practice.stem: A 55 year old woman has haemorrhoids that are permanently prolapsed and cannot be pushed back. They bleed and ache daily. Banding twice has failed. Colonoscopy was normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Irreducible (grade 4) haemorrhoids, especially after failed banding, need haemorrhoidectomy.

steps.x: Definitive management for the top grade.
Grade 4 after failed banding: surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Haemorrhoidectomy.**
**A. Haemorrhoidectomy.** Grade 3–4 severe = haemorrhoidectomy.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has rubber band ligation of an internal haemorrhoid in clinic without anaesthetic. He feels only a dull ache. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which best explains why the procedure is painless?
o: Columnar epithelium has no blood supply
Pudendal nerve supply above the dentate line
Squamous epithelium above the dentate line
The band blocks the pudendal nerve
Visceral innervation above the dentate line
practice.e: Internal haemorrhoids lie above the dentate line, where innervation is visceral, so banding causes only a dull ache.

steps.x: Applied anatomy of the dentate line.
Above the dentate line: columnar mucosa, visceral (autonomic) nerves.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Visceral innervation above the dentate line.**

elim: Squamous epithelium is below the line.

steps.x: **E. Visceral innervation above the dentate line.** Above = visceral, painless; below = somatic, painful.
